title: A Taxonomy for Next-gen Reasoning — Nathan Lambert, Allen Institute (AI2) & Interconnects.ai
talk_summary: Nathan Lambert proposes a taxonomy for next-gen reasoning models: skills (math/code), calibration (matching token spend to difficulty), strategy (going the right direction), and abstraction (breaking hard tasks into tractable subtasks). He argues planning is the next frontier and that overthinking/calibration is already a major cost and latency problem for products.

takeaways.technique: Calibrate reasoning effort to task difficulty
takeaways.what_they_do: Reasoning models overthink trivial problems, spending hundreds to thousands of tokens on questions answerable in one token; products should route effort by difficulty rather than always maxing reasoning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can ask a language model like what is 2 plus 3 and you can see these reasoning models use hundreds to a thousand tokens
takeaways.numbers: 10 to 100x token spend when shipping to a reasoning model; hundreds to 1000 tokens for 2+3

takeaways.what_they_do: Models currently dive straight into solving without sketching a plan; adding an explicit plan phase before reasoning/answer tokens improves direction and avoids wasting large token budgets going the wrong way.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it just goes right in and it doesn't anything like trying to sketch the problem before it thinks
takeaways.numbers: 10 to 40,000 tokens per attempt if direction is wrong

takeaways.what_they_do: Running multiple attempts in parallel and selecting/merging makes answers more robust and better-crafted, distinct from single-chain inference scaling; models could themselves spawn parallel sub-calls.
takeaways.evidence_quote: people are spinning up t-mucks and launching cloud code in 10 windows to do this themselves

takeaways.what_they_do: Long-horizon agents need a defined policy for compressing memory when context fills, avoiding repeated mistakes, and offloading hard subproblems; current compression choices are ad hoc.
takeaways.evidence_quote: cloud code compresses its memory when it fills up its context window. We don't know if that's the optimal way

takeaways.what_they_do: Filter training/eval questions by base-model difficulty: discard tasks solved 0/100 or 100/100 times because they waste compute and add noise.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if a question is solved zero out of 100 times by your base model or 100 out of 100, you don't want questions

takeaways.technique: Effort selectors as a product concern
takeaways.what_they_do: Reasoning-effort selectors are pushed to users and are 'rough'; the model should know how much effort to spend so users don't overspend tokens or switch providers.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there's these reasoning effort selectors in the API and this is really rough on a user side of things
